test_title: SSC MTS 2025 Official Paper (Held On: 05 Feb, 2026 Shift 1)
subject: general
question:
In the given question, a sentence is divided into four parts and given in the alternatives (A), (B), (C), and (D). There is an error in one part. Choose the alternative containing that part of the sentence that has the error. Choosing the alternative with the error will be the answer.

The Golden Temple was crowded by millions of devotees from all around the world on the day of Baisakhi.
solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error lies in the prepositional usage in the phrase "**crowded by**."
 
• In English, the verb "**crowd**" (when used in the passive voice to describe a space being full) is conventionally followed by the preposition "**with**."
 
• The phrase "**crowded with**" is a standard collocation used to indicate that a place is packed or filled with a particular group of people or things.
 
• Thus, the correct preposition should be "**with**" instead of "**by**."

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"The Golden Temple was **crowded with** millions of devotees from all around the world on the day of Baisakhi."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: "The Golden Temple was"** – This part is correct; it establishes the subject and the passive voice auxiliary verb.
 
• **Option 3: "from all around the world"** – This is a grammatically sound prepositional phrase used to denote the origin of the devotees.
 
• **Option 4: "on the day of Baisakhi."** – This is correct; "on" is the appropriate preposition used for specific days or dates.
 
• **Confusing Prepositions:** While "by" is often used in passive voice to denote the agent of an action (e.g., "eaten by"), when describing the state of being full, "with" is the idiomatic choice (e.g., "filled with," "packed with," "crowded with").
